title: Lake Bogoria: Hot Springs, Geysers and Flamingos in Kenya's Rift Valley
meta_title: Lake Bogoria Guide: 7 Things to Know Before You Go
meta_description: Lake Bogoria guide: what the hot springs, geysers and flamingos look like now, how to get there, the best time to go and what to pair it with.
excerpt: Lake Bogoria is a steaming soda lake in Kenya's Rift Valley. This guide covers the hot springs, the drowned geysers, flamingos, getting there and the best time to visit.
content:
Lake Bogoria is a shallow soda lake in Kenya's Rift Valley, about 240 km north of Nairobi, famous for steaming hot springs, spouting geysers and flocks of lesser flamingos. Rising water has drowned many of its geysers since 2012, yet the hot springs, birdlife and dramatic escarpment still make it a rewarding stop on a Rift Valley safari.

Most guides online still describe the lake as it looked a decade ago, so travellers arrive expecting a field of geysers and a sea of pink. This guide gives you the honest current picture, how to get there, when to go, what you can still see and how to combine the reserve with Lake Baringo and Lake Nakuru.

Quick Facts

  • Location: Baringo County, Kenya, about 240 km north of Nairobi and 120 km north of Nakuru
  • Protected since: National reserve from 1973; Ramsar wetland from 2001; part of the Kenya Lake System World Heritage Site since 2011
  • Reserve size: About 10,700 hectares, including the lake and its shoreline woodland
  • Altitude: Roughly 990 m above sea level, so it is hot for most of the year
  • Hot springs: Around 200 springs recorded along the shore, with vent water close to boiling
  • Wildlife highlights: Lesser flamingos, greater kudu and rich water birdlife
  • Best paired with: Lake Baringo (about 35 km away) and Lake Nakuru National Park

What Is Lake Bogoria Famous For?

Lake Bogoria is famous for three things: hot springs and geysers along its western shore, large gatherings of lesser flamingos that feed on algae in the alkaline water, and the wall of the Siracho escarpment rising above its eastern side. Few places in Africa show the Rift Valley's volcanic heat so clearly.

The lake sits in a narrow trough of the Rift, around 17 km long and only a few kilometres wide. It has no outlet, so water evaporates and leaves a strongly alkaline, salty lake. That chemistry suits spirulina-type algae, which in turn feeds the flamingos.

The reserve was gazetted in 1973 and listed as a Ramsar wetland of international importance in 2001. The Ramsar site record for Lake Bogoria notes that the wetland can support up to 1.5 million migratory birds and highlights the greater kudu living in its shoreline acacia woodland. In 2011, Bogoria joined Lake Nakuru and Lake Elementaita in the Kenya Lake System World Heritage Site.

The Loburu hot springs

The main hot spring field is at Loburu, on the western shore. Here water bubbles out of the ground and runs into the lake in steaming channels, with orange and green bands of heat-loving algae along the edges. Scientists have recorded water reaching up to 99 degrees Celsius at some vents, so the ground near the springs can be dangerous.

A second group of springs lies further south near Chemurkeu. Guides keep visitors on firm ground and away from thin crusts, which can break over scalding water.

Are There Still Geysers at Lake Bogoria?

The lake still has hot springs and a few small spouting vents, but most of its famous geysers are now underwater. The lake has risen steadily since around 2012 after years of heavy rain, and the reserve's senior warden told Kenya's Nation newspaper in 2025 that about 90 percent of the geysers had been submerged.

NASA's Earth Observatory reported in 2020 that the lake had grown by about a quarter and that nearly 80 percent of its hot springs were already under water. The rise has continued since. In July 2026, the warden reported that the old entry gate and much of the road from it, plus the Emsos gate road towards Mogotio, were underwater.

What this means for you: expect steam rising from the shallows and active springs on the remaining shoreline rather than tall jets. Some springs now bubble up through the lake itself, which is striking in its own way. Routes inside the reserve change as the water moves, so travel with a driver who knows the current access roads.

How the rising water affects a Lake Bogoria visit

The flooding has also cost the reserve campsites and facilities, and visitor numbers fell sharply. That is a reason to visit with clear expectations rather than to skip it. The lake is quieter than ever, the scenery is still dramatic, and park revenue supports a community that has lost land to the water.

When Is the Best Time to Visit Lake Bogoria?

The best time to visit is during the drier months, roughly January to February and June to October, when roads are firmer and the hot springs steam clearly in the cool early morning. Flamingo numbers depend on algae and water levels rather than the calendar, so no month guarantees a big flock.

The long rains usually fall from March to May and the short rains around November. Rain makes murram roads slippery and can cut off tracks near the shore. Heat is the other factor: at about 990 m the lake basin is warm all year, so plan walks for early morning and late afternoon.

How Do You Get to Lake Bogoria from Nairobi?

The reserve is reached by road from Nairobi via Nakuru, a journey of about 240 km heading north through the Rift Valley. Allow a long half day with a stop, which is why most travellers stay overnight nearby or visit from a base at Lake Baringo or Nakuru rather than doing a return day trip.

From Nakuru the road continues north towards Marigat, the small town between Bogoria and Baringo. The two lakes are about 35 km apart, so you can see the hot springs in the morning and take a boat on Lake Baringo the same afternoon.

Can you do Lake Bogoria as a day trip?

A day trip from Nairobi is possible but tiring, with most of the day spent driving. A better plan is two or three nights in the region, adding Lake Nakuru on the way. Our guide to a Lake Nakuru day trip from Nairobi explains how that park fits into the same route.

Entry fees and paperwork

Lake Bogoria National Reserve is managed by Baringo County, not the Kenya Wildlife Service, so it has its own gate fees, with different rates for non-residents, Kenya residents and citizens. Fees change, so we confirm the current rate when we quote your trip. Carry your passport, as you would for any Kenyan reserve.

Things to Do at Lake Bogoria

The main things to do here are watching the hot springs, looking for flamingos and other water birds, spotting greater kudu in the southern woodland and enjoying the views of the escarpment. It is a nature and scenery stop rather than a Big Five game drive.

Flamingo watching

Lesser flamingos gather where the algae is richest, and their numbers swing widely. The same Nation report noted the population had fallen from over 1.5 million to around 500,000, with many birds moving to other lakes in 2024 before numbers began to rise again in 2025. Some days you will see thousands; on others only scattered groups.

Greater kudu and other wildlife

The acacia woodland along the shore is home to greater kudu, a large antelope with long spiralled horns that is uncommon in most Kenyan parks. The Ramsar listing names the kudu as one of the reserve's key species. Scan the bush edges slowly in the early morning, when they come out to browse.

Birding around the lake

Beyond flamingos, the shoreline and nearby swamps attract waders, ducks and birds of prey. Keen birders often combine Bogoria with Lake Baringo, which has a very different freshwater bird list. Our birding safaris in East Africa are built around exactly this kind of lake-hopping route.

Lake Bogoria vs Lake Nakuru and Lake Baringo: Which Should You Visit?

Bogoria is best for hot springs and raw Rift Valley scenery, Lake Nakuru for rhinos and classic game drives, and Lake Baringo for freshwater birding and boat trips. Each is different enough that many travellers visit two or all three on one route.

Lake BogoriaSoda (alkaline)Hot springs, flamingos, greater kudu, escarpment viewsGeology lovers, photographers, birders
Lake NakuruSoda (alkaline)Rhinos, lions, buffalo, viewpointsFirst-time safari travellers and families
Lake BaringoFreshBoat rides, hippos, crocodiles, island hot springsBirders and relaxed lakeside stays

For the full park picture, read our Lake Nakuru National Park guide. If you are heading further north after the lakes, the Rift Valley road links well with Samburu National Reserve or the conservancies of the Laikipia wilderness.

How Many Days Do You Need for Lake Bogoria?

The reserve itself needs a half day to a full day, but the region deserves two or three nights so that you are not rushing long drives. A relaxed Rift Valley lakes loop from Nairobi usually takes three days, and it slots neatly before or after a Masai Mara safari.

Sample three-day Rift Valley lakes route

  • Day 1: Nairobi to Lake Nakuru National Park for an afternoon game drive, overnight in Nakuru.
  • Day 2: Early drive north to Lake Bogoria for the hot springs and flamingos, then on to Lake Baringo for a sunset boat ride, overnight at Baringo.
  • Day 3: Morning birding at Lake Baringo, then drive back to Nairobi or continue to Laikipia or Samburu.

Is It Safe to Visit the Lake Bogoria Hot Springs?

The Lake Bogoria hot springs are safe to visit if you stay on firm, marked ground and follow your guide. The danger is the water itself: vents can approach boiling point, and the crust around some springs is thin. Never step onto wet, discoloured ground or let children run ahead near the springs.

Swimming in the lake is not recommended. The water is strongly alkaline and very warm near the springs, and submerged vents are hard to see now that the lake has risen. Wear closed shoes, carry plenty of drinking water, use sun protection and keep valuables zipped away from steam and spray.

Insider Tips

  • Go early: Arrive soon after the gate opens, when the steam is thickest and the heat is bearable.
  • Set expectations: Think steaming springs and Rift scenery, not tall geysers; flamingo numbers vary from week to week.
  • Use a local driver: Shoreline tracks move as the water rises, so local knowledge saves time and avoids flooded roads.
  • Pack for heat: Hat, sunscreen, 2 litres of water per person and closed shoes for warm, uneven ground.
  • Bring binoculars: Flamingos often feed far out, and the kudu are shy.
  • Pair it well: Combine with Lake Baringo the same day for a contrast between soda and freshwater lakes.

Who Will Enjoy Lake Bogoria Most?

Bogoria suits travellers who enjoy landscapes, geology, photography and birds, and repeat visitors to Kenya who have already done the big game parks. It suits less well a short first safari focused on lions and elephants, where the time is better spent in the Masai Mara.

It also works well for Nairobi residents and expatriates looking for a long-weekend road trip into the Rift. If you like quiet, off-the-beaten-track places, read our guide to Kakamega Forest, another western Kenya gem that rewards curious travellers.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Lake Bogoria worth visiting?

Lake Bogoria is worth visiting if you enjoy dramatic scenery, hot springs, birds and quieter places. Most of its geysers are now underwater after years of rising water, but steaming springs, flamingos and greater kudu remain. It works best as part of a Rift Valley lakes route with Lake Baringo and Lake Nakuru, not as a stand-alone trip.

How far is Lake Bogoria from Nairobi?

Lake Bogoria is about 240 km north of Nairobi, reached by road through Nakuru and on towards Marigat. Allow a long half day each way with a stop. Because of the distance, most travellers stay overnight at Lake Baringo or Nakuru instead of attempting a tiring return day trip from Nairobi.

Can you swim in Lake Bogoria?

Swimming in Lake Bogoria is not recommended. The water is strongly alkaline and salty, and hot springs along the shore can reach close to boiling point. Since the lake rose, some vents are hidden under the surface, which adds to the risk. Enjoy the springs from firm ground with a guide and save swimming for your lodge pool.

Are there still flamingos at Lake Bogoria?

Lake Bogoria still attracts lesser flamingos, but numbers rise and fall with algae and water levels. Reports in 2025 put the population at around 500,000, down from more than 1.5 million, after many birds moved to other lakes in 2024. Some visits bring thousands of birds, others only scattered groups, so treat flamingos as a bonus.

What is the best time to visit Lake Bogoria?

The best time to visit is during the drier months, roughly January to February and June to October. Roads are firmer and early mornings show the hot springs steaming clearly. The long rains from March to May can make tracks muddy. Flamingo numbers do not follow a fixed season, so no month guarantees a large flock.

Final Thoughts

Bogoria is still one of Kenya's most unusual places: a hot, steaming soda lake beneath the Rift escarpment, with flamingos, kudu and springs close to boiling. Go with honest expectations about the drowned geysers and pair it with Lake Baringo and Lake Nakuru for a rewarding few days.
